A1.justification: The authors, retained Gaussian/MPM pipeline, scenes and weather tasks identify the same research work despite the changed title and substantial redesign. Both PDFs provide readable main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices; rendered pages resolve extraction issues.

before.justification: v1 reports original weather and object simulations, quantitative comparisons with ClimateNeRF and GaussCtrl in Table 1, and qualitative collision-handling ablations and baseline comparisons.

after.justification: v2 reports original weather-generation experiments, image/video metric comparisons, an adapted Instruct-4DGS comparison, and quantitative component, regularization and trajectory-drift ablations in Tables 1–6.

M1.justification: v1 directly renders simulated motion using manually specified or GaussianDreamer-derived appearance. v2 introduces LLM initialization and recurrent neural dynamics jointly optimized through Video-SDS, physics/appearance regularization and adaptive weighting, retaining simulation as a motion prior. Appendix B.2 also adds ClimateNeRF-supervised background-snow finetuning.

E1.justification: The five scenes from Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks and Temples and the four weather effects remain. However, v2 removes the distinct structured-object tasks demonstrated in v1: falling leaves/feathers and landing drones, UFOs and bees. v2 instead presents text-guided appearance variants such as purple snow and magic particles, replacing the earlier manual controllability demonstrations.

E2.justification: ClimateNeRF and GaussCtrl remain in the weather comparison. v2 adds an evaluated, adapted Instruct-4DGS dynamic editing baseline with qualitative results and Table 3, while removing v1's AutoVFX comparison on feather/drone effects. This substantially changes the dynamic comparison evidence.

E3.justification: v2 adds ViCLIP-T and VE-Bench evaluation using 15 interpolated camera trajectories per scene, plus average trajectory drift for new ablations. The stated weather simulation length changes from 250 to 500 steps. The new Instruct-4DGS experiment trains a zero-initialized deformation field and specifies 3,000/5,000 optimization iterations. These introduce materially different evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: v1 provides a qualitative collision-handling ablation. v2 expands this into four qualitative and quantitative component variants, then adds fixed-versus-adaptive weighting, individual regularization-loss removal and trajectory-drift sensitivity studies (Table 2 and Appendix A, Tables 4–6). These test optimization mechanisms and failure conditions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Neither version documents repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's average trajectory drift is an evaluation metric, and its discussion of diffusion uncertainty motivates weighting; neither establishes experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the proposed method's all-weather CLIPSim/CLIPDir/VQAScore values of 0.25/0.09/0.80 with 0.28/0.11/0.89; the corresponding baseline image scores remain unchanged. v2 adds video scores, dynamic-baseline results and extensive ablation/drift findings, while removing object-animation results. The changed method and simulation duration prevent interpreting the higher scores as controlled same-setting gains.

T1.justification: v2 introduces mathematical definitions for recurrent velocity, position, rotation and appearance updates and the combined Video-SDS/physics/appearance objective (Equations 5–8). These substantially extend v1's rendering, simulation-update and active-tracking formulation. v2 also explicitly assumes learned trajectories remain close to the simulation prior. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a three-stage Gaussian/particle simulation framework with specialized collisions and object-animation extensions to physics-guided score distillation and joint learned motion/appearance refinement. The abstract, introduction and conclusion newly claim that physics guidance and joint refinement are essential for coherent multi-particle generation; the structured-object generality claim disappears.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking recurrent error accumulation and trajectory drift to regularization, including the tradeoff between insufficient and excessive physics constraints. Its ablations identify appearance regularization as critical and rotation regularization as relatively unimportant. The earlier manual-appearance mismatch limitation is replaced by limitations involving environmental lighting responses and unreliable guidance after trajectory divergence; the bidirectional-interaction limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds neural architecture, CogVideoX-2B optimization settings, regularization weights, Claude Sonnet 4 initialization, prompts and evaluation details. Explicit manual appearance values and GaussianDreamer instructions from v1 disappear. Resource reporting changes from A5000 simulation/rendering at 7 FPS to A100 execution with approximately two minutes of simulation, one hour of optimization and subsequent rendering at 10 FPS; these describe different workloads.

R1.justification: Research positioning is reorganized around score distillation, static editing and physics animation to motivate joint optimization. v2 adds substantial coverage of methods including Instruct-NeRF2NeRF, GaussianEditor and Instruct4D-to-4D/Instruct-4DGS, alongside video-diffusion and evaluation references. AutoVFX, GaussianDreamer and much of the earlier classical simulation and mesh-editing discussion are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements and conclusion are extensively rewritten around physics-guided score distillation. The method narrative changes from three simulation/rendering stages to a motion prior plus learned optimization. Related work is reordered, and the appendices are reorganized into additional experiments, technical details and visual results.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to show the neural optimization loop. The controllability and ablation displays are replaced or expanded, Table 1 gains video-metric columns, and Tables 2–6 and new experimental figures are added. Object-animation and AutoVFX figures disappear. The earlier appendix comparison figures are updated and relocated as Figures 11–12, rather than wholly new comparisons.

improvement.justification: v1's dynamic-realism claims relied on image metrics and a narrow qualitative ablation. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through video metrics, a dynamic editing comparator, quantitative component and sensitivity studies, and explicit failure analysis, with much fuller optimization documentation. These gains outweigh reduced object-task coverage and added optimization cost. Performance attribution remains limited by changed simulation settings, absent uncertainty estimates and ClimateNeRF-supervised background snow, but the overall evidential and explanatory improvement is substantial.
